title: The Great Recession

jokes.text: Do you think maybe he's just vacationing, though?
jokes.setup: An RV is parked outside with blocks in front and back of its tires, clearly indicating the owner is living there permanently.
jokes.punchline: Charlie genuinely suggests the person might just be on vacation, revealing his obliviousness.
jokes.explanation: Classic Charlie obliviousness deployed efficiently in one line. The wheel blocks detail makes his vacation theory immediately absurd. Strong character integration — only Charlie would miss something this obvious.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Ever since the recession hit, waves of new people are suddenly broke. These people have no idea how to live without money. They're what's called 'new poor.' We're old poor.

jokes.text: once all the other RV folks see what this RV guy's doing, they're going to start parking their RVs on our street and we're going to be staring down the barrel of a shanty town situation.
jokes.setup: One RV is parked on the street.
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately escalates to full shantytown apocalypse in his head, delivered with complete seriousness.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from one RV to shantytown is a good character beat for Mac's catastrophizing. The phrase 'shantytown situation' is funny in its bureaucratic framing. Sets up a running gag for the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Have some class if you're gonna be poor!

jokes.text: I'll tell you who. The new poor. / Ever since the recession hit, waves of new people are suddenly broke. These people have no idea how to live without money. They're what's called 'new poor.' We're old poor.
jokes.setup: The gang is outraged about the RV person displaying their homelessness publicly.
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers a straight-faced sociological breakdown distinguishing 'new poor' from 'old poor,' positioning themselves — people who run a barely-functional dive bar — as the aristocracy of poverty.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest jokes. The concept of 'old poor vs. new poor' is a brilliantly original inversion — the gang has zero self-awareness that their claim to poverty dignity is itself absurd. Dennis's authoritative delivery of a made-up sociological category is pitch-perfect character work. 'We're old poor' as a point of PRIDE is the kind of dark, specific absurdism Always Sunny excels at. Highly quotable and earns its score.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Well, you start putting plans under microscopes, nothing's gonna make sense, all right?

jokes.text: No, have some class if you're going to be poor.
jokes.setup: Dennis has established the 'old poor' framework; Mac follows up.
jokes.punchline: Mac earnestly advises the homeless person to have class — as if poverty etiquette is a real standard being violated.
jokes.explanation: A solid button on the 'old poor' joke. 'Have some class if you're going to be poor' is a funny line that extends the irony, though it's clearly the second beat to a superior setup.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Dee! Sharpest item in the bar! I need it now! Let's go!

jokes.text: Let's slash his tires. / Well, not that, though, because then he can't leave — that doesn't make any sense.
jokes.setup: The gang decides to send the RV guy a message and make him leave.
jokes.punchline: Mac's solution to making someone leave is to slash their tires — the one thing that guarantees they cannot leave.
jokes.explanation: Clean and efficient joke with solid structure. The idiocy of the plan is immediately apparent to Dennis (and the audience), and his deadpan 'that doesn't make any sense' sells it. Good gang-stupidity comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: His neck is so thick, I feel like he's just gonna swing and dangle around for a really long time.

jokes.text: Well, you start putting plans under microscopes and nothing's gonna make sense, all right?
jokes.setup: Dennis points out that slashing tires so someone can leave makes no sense.
jokes.punchline: Mac's defense is that ALL plans fall apart under scrutiny — therefore scrutiny is the problem, not the bad plan.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. It's a perfect encapsulation of Mac's anti-intellectual self-protection — rather than admit the plan is bad, he attacks the concept of critical analysis itself. The logic is internally consistent in its wrongness, which is what makes it great. Highly quotable, could be lifted to any context. Earns its 8.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Frank, it's not gonna work for you. Your neck's too thick, buddy.

jokes.text: Dee, sharpest item in the bar — I need it now! Let's go! / Oh, Frank's trying to kill himself.
jokes.setup: Dennis urgently demands the sharpest item in the bar — implying a weapon or tool for the RV conflict.
jokes.punchline: Mac flatly reveals the reason: Frank is attempting suicide in the bar.
jokes.explanation: Sharp misdirection: 'sharpest item in the bar' implies the RV conflict, then Mac's completely flat 'Oh, Frank's trying to kill himself' is a perfect non-reaction that tells us everything about these characters. The casualness of Mac's delivery is the entire joke.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Maybe we should take this time to streamline Paddy's, make it run as efficiently as the government.

jokes.text: His neck is so thick. I feel like he's just going to swing and dangle around for a really long time.
jokes.setup: Frank is hanging from a noose, having lost all his money. The gang considers cutting him down.
jokes.punchline: Rather than express concern, Charlie clinically analyzes why the hanging won't work due to Frank's neck thickness.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely dark and funny — Charlie is not horrified, he's doing physics. The specificity of 'swing and dangle around for a really long time' is what makes it land. Classic Always Sunny moral vacuum humor.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Frank, don't be a moron. You start cutting bonuses, you're gonna lose your top guys.

jokes.text: No, no, no, no, pull my leg. / Frank, it's not going to work for you. Your neck's too thick, buddy.
jokes.setup: Frank is hanging and the gang is debating cutting him down.
jokes.punchline: Frank asks them to pull his legs to help the hanging work; Mac responds practically by confirming the anatomical problem.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Frank's desperation (asking for leg-pulling assistance) paired with Mac's clinical confirmation of the neck problem continues the dark absurdism of the hanging scene perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: No, we're chaff.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: No, we're not. We're- We're wheat.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Why would you want to be wheat?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Why would you ever want to be chaff?

jokes.text: Tie a chair to me. Tie a chair to me.
jokes.setup: Frank's hanging isn't working due to his thick neck; Mac has just confirmed this.
jokes.punchline: Frank's solution is to request additional weight via a chair — still fully committed to the plan.
jokes.explanation: Frank problem-solving his own suicide in real-time is a great joke. The repetition ('Tie a chair to me. Tie a chair to me.') adds urgency and desperation. Very Sunny in its commitment to the bit.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: We have no business sense? He's the one dangling from a noose 10 minutes ago.

jokes.text: Frank, if you're looking for a better steak in an arcade setting, you are shit out of luck.
jokes.setup: Frank says 'this is terrible.' Mac assumes he means the Dave & Buster's experience.
jokes.punchline: Mac's sincere defense of D&B's steak quality reveals he entirely missed Frank's serious financial concern — and also that he has earnest opinions about Dave & Buster's cuisine.
jokes.explanation: A great misdirect: 'this is terrible' should pivot to the financial crisis, but Mac's specific, heartfelt defense of Dave & Buster's as a steakhouse is both surprising and perfectly in character. The phrase 'in an arcade setting' as a qualifying criterion for steak quality is delightfully specific.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Dee, we don't know what it is that you do around here. You don't seem to do anything.

jokes.text: It's only fair that the upper management of the bar get together to talk shop over notch steak and some video games.
jokes.setup: Frank is in financial crisis and criticizing expense meals.
jokes.punchline: Mac describes himself and Dennis as 'upper management' who deserve steak-and-video-game meetings as a reasonable business expense.
jokes.explanation: A reliable character beat — Mac's grandiose self-regard is a well-worn joke on the show. Functional but not exceptional. The D&B's context adds some flavor.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: But the mountains, they've turned blue.

jokes.text: If anything, we should be talking about bonuses. / Let's talk bonuses. That's a good idea.
jokes.setup: Frank warns them the business is failing and they need to cut costs.
jokes.punchline: Dennis pivots to demanding bonuses; Mac immediately enthusiastically co-signs.
jokes.explanation: Solid irony — demanding bonuses during a financial crisis is a timely joke (2009 recession context). The quick Mac echo adds rhythm. Not original but lands well.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I quit.

jokes.text: You got to separate the wheat from the chaff somehow. / And these dudes are all chaff. / Yeah. / Well, no, we're all wheat. / No, we're chaff. / No, we're not. We're wheat. / Why would you want to be wheat? / Why would you ever want to be chaff?
jokes.setup: Frank uses the 'wheat from the chaff' idiom to suggest cutting underperformers.
jokes.punchline: Dennis and Mac don't know what wheat or chaff mean, devolving into an argument about which is preferable based purely on the sounds of the words.
jokes.explanation: A great little routine showing the guys' stupidity without being too broad. The beat where Dennis declares 'we're all wheat' and Mac contradicts 'no, we're chaff' — with neither knowing the meaning — is a funny two-beat rhythm. Frank's exasperated dismissal lands the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I am taking it to the furnace... This bar runs on trash.

jokes.text: We have no business sense? He's the one dangling from a noose ten minutes ago.
jokes.setup: Frank calls Dennis and Mac idiots with no business sense.
jokes.punchline: Mac counters by reminding everyone Frank was hanging himself from a noose very recently.
jokes.explanation: A well-timed callback that works both as a comeback and as a reminder of the show's moral darkness — the noose incident was 10 minutes ago and everyone has already moved on to business disputes. The specificity of 'ten minutes ago' sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Well, I could put the trash into a landfill where it's gonna stay for millions of years, or I could burn it up and get a nice, smoky smell in here and let that smoke go into the sky where it turns into stars.

jokes.text: Frank, you're out. You're fired. / Oh! You just got squeezed out, bitch!
jokes.setup: Mac's noose callback lands as a good point; Dennis immediately seizes the moment.
jokes.punchline: They fire Frank — the man who owns/bankrolls the bar — and Mac erupts with 'You just got squeezed out, bitch!'
jokes.explanation: Mac's triumphant 'squeezed out, bitch!' is a fun character moment — his love of dramatic declarations. The absurdity of them firing the person who bankrolls everything is a good ironic beat.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: That doesn't sound right, but I don't know enough about stars to dispute it.

jokes.text: You're firing us? / Well, first we're going to give you the opportunity to defend your jobs. / Really? / Yeah. / All right. I appreciate the opportunity, fellas. / All right. / I'm on it. Whoo!
jokes.setup: Dennis and Mac call in Charlie and Dee to defend their jobs, expecting to flex power.
jokes.punchline: Charlie instantly accepts the premise with genuine, eager positivity — 'I appreciate the opportunity, fellas. I'm on it. Whoo!' — immediately deflating Dennis's power move.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's genuine enthusiasm for proving himself, combined with his complete ignorance of the power dynamic, is a good character beat. The 'Whoo!' caps it nicely.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Charlie, that sign does not say 'Coors.'... It says 'closed,' Charlie!

jokes.text: Nobody orders a mojito in this bar. / So, you can't make a mojito. / Of course I can make a mojito.
jokes.setup: Dee is asked to mix a drink to prove she can do her job; Dennis asks for a mojito.
jokes.punchline: Dee's defense ('nobody orders a mojito') implies she's never made one; Dennis immediately calls it out; Dee doubles down despite clearly not being able to.
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy. Dee's incompetence plus defensiveness is a reliable character beat. Not particularly original but the rhythm of the exchange works.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: So you're gonna throw all the trash in the furnace yourselves. And you're gonna filter the rainwater barrel all by yourselves... and siphon it from all around the neighborhood.

jokes.text: No, not a beer. Something you have to mix. / But this bottle is cold-activated. I mean, look at it. Doesn't that look delicious? / It does look delicious, but mix me a drink. / But the mountains, they've turned blue.
jokes.setup: Dennis asks Dee to mix a drink to test her competency as a bartender.
jokes.punchline: Dee attempts to sell the Coors Light cold-activation as a valid alternative to actually mixing anything, with increasing desperation about the blue mountains.
jokes.explanation: Dee's escalating fixation on the cold-activation gimmick as a substitute for actual competence is both funny and character-specific. 'The mountains, they've turned blue' as a last-ditch argument is a great comedic beat. Lightly satirizes Coors Light advertising while revealing Dee's desperation.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: We're gonna call a trash man, an electrician, and a plumber and not turn the closed sign on when the bar is open!

jokes.text: I quit. / Goddamn it. Shit. / I was really looking forward to firing her. / Me, too.
jokes.setup: Dee is about to fail at making a mojito and be fired.
jokes.punchline: Dee quits before they can fire her, and Dennis and Mac express genuine disappointment that they were robbed of the pleasure of firing someone.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly structured two-beat joke. Dee's self-preservation quits defuses their power play, then Mac and Dennis's synchronized disappointment at being denied the firing reveals their cruelty. 'Me, too' as a quiet echo sells the joke with great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Honey, I'm home! Feast your eyes on the new headquarters of Reynolds and Reynolds.

jokes.text: Charlie burns trash in the furnace to heat the bar and generate 'a nice smoky smell.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are auditing Charlie's job duties; Charlie explains his trash disposal method.
jokes.punchline: Charlie burns garbage in the bar's furnace, believing this is both green and an aromatic amenity ('a good smoky smell that we all like').
jokes.explanation: A great Charlie revelation — the audience learns the bar has been running on garbage combustion. His framing of trash-burning as an amenity ('the good smoky smell that we all like') is simultaneously gross and funny. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Well, what the hell, dude? I don't know if I can live in a trailer, man.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You don't have to, Charlie. It's kinda tight in there already.

jokes.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Well, I could put the trash into a landfill where it's going to stay for millions of years, or I could burn it up and get a nice smoky smell in here and let that smoke go into the sky where it turns into stars.
jokes.setup: Mac tells Charlie that burning trash is 'the exact opposite of green.'
jokes.punchline: Charlie's environmental counter-argument concludes with the genuinely baffling claim that smoke turns into stars.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode and a classic Always Sunny Charlie moment. The build from (imperfect) environmental argument to the magnificent logical leap that 'smoke turns into stars' is extraordinary. It's Charlie's cosmology — a universe where garbage incineration is star formation. The delivery of an absurd conclusion with the same earnest confidence as the preceding (almost defensible) argument is brilliant character work. Only Charlie Kelly could arrive at this. Quotable, iconic, earns 8.5+ craft.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: We're not in the business of giving out handouts, Charlie. We're not the government.

jokes.text: That doesn't sound right, but I don't know enough about stars to dispute it. / No, it's right.
jokes.setup: Charlie claims smoke turns into stars.
jokes.punchline: Mac, unable to refute the claim on scientific grounds, essentially accepts it. Charlie immediately confirms it.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the stars joke. Mac's scientific agnosticism ('I don't know enough about stars to dispute it') is a great character beat — he won't accept it but he won't reject it either. Charlie's immediate 'No, it's right' is the ideal response. Economical and devastating.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: That's a $200 shoe!

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Look at that. Feast your eyes on your new business. Knives.

jokes.text: Charlie has been turning on the 'Closed' sign every morning to let people know they have cold Coors in the bar.
jokes.setup: Charlie describes his final morning task: turning on the Coors sign to invite customers in.
jokes.punchline: The sign says 'CLOSED' — Charlie has been advertising the bar as closed every morning for apparently years.
jokes.explanation: A great visual/structural joke. The setup is a full minute of Charlie building toward 'and then, lastly, I turn on the Coors sign' with authority and pride. The reveal that it says CLOSED — and that he's apparently been doing this for however long — is a perfect slow-build payoff. The audience realizes simultaneously with Mac and Dennis. 'You can't really read it from the inside' is an outstanding button that earns its own score.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You want me to sell knives door-to-door?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: No. You're selling vacuums.

jokes.text: Okay. Yeah, right, I can see that now, but you know, you can't really read it from the inside. / You can't read it from the outside.
jokes.setup: Charlie's 'Coors sign' is revealed to say 'CLOSED.'
jokes.punchline: Charlie's defense is that it's hard to read from inside the bar; Dennis notes it's also impossible to read correctly from outside.
jokes.explanation: The button on the Closed sign reveal. Charlie's self-justification ('can't read it from inside') immediately countered by Dennis's correction ('can't read it from outside either') — a clean two-beat structure that wrings one more laugh from the gag.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Oh! [Shouts]

jokes.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Oh, really? Oh, so you're going to throw all the trash in the furnace yourselves and you're going to filter the rainwater barrel all by yourselves and I suppose you're going to fiddle with the electricity every day, all by yourselves, and you're going to siphon it from all around the neighborhood?
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis fire Charlie; he pushes back.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's list of indispensable job duties escalates from bizarre to criminal: filtering rainwater, fiddling with electricity, and finally — siphoning electricity from the neighborhood.
jokes.explanation: Classic Charlie escalation monologue. Each item is worse than the last — the list is a perfect revelation of how the bar actually operates. The pivot from trash/rainwater (questionable) to 'siphoning electricity from around the neighborhood' (criminal) is the ideal comedic escalation. Strongly character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Mine does not, and believe me, I've tried at several locations...

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: There's one in Franklin Mills I haven't tried. I feel like that could maybe work.

jokes.text: No, we're going to call a trash man and an electrician and a plumber and not turn the 'closed' sign on when the bar is open.
jokes.setup: Charlie insists his bizarre job tasks are indispensable.
jokes.punchline: Mac's rebuttal is a list of normal solutions plus — as the final item — the callback that they simply won't turn the Closed sign on.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback button — lumping 'not turning on the closed sign' in with legitimate business solutions makes it land as an understatement. The list structure builds well.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: It doesn't work anywhere else. It's only gonna work here...

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Then afterwards, we'll go out to Fox Chase and use the Power Card at that Friday's out there.

jokes.text: Full-blown shantytown. We're screwed.
jokes.setup: Earlier Mac predicted a shantytown if more RVs arrived.
jokes.punchline: His prophecy has come true — more RVs/displaced people have arrived.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying payoff on Mac's shantytown prophecy. Brief, well-timed. The word 'full-blown' is a good modifier. Not a big laugh but structurally earned.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: What are you talking about? You don't make house payments. You own this house. You've owned it for years. Mom, that's crazy. You collect Social Security.

jokes.text: Honey, I'm home. / Feast your eyes on the new headquarters of Reynolds & Reynolds. / Frank and I are starting a business. We sublet our apartments. We're living in here.
jokes.setup: Dee has just quit her job and gone to Frank for rent money.
jokes.punchline: Frank reveals he has sublet both their apartments and is now living in the RV shantytown — the very thing they were outraged about at the episode's start.
jokes.explanation: Ironic payoff: Frank and Dee, who were furious at the new poor RV dwellers, have now themselves become new poor RV dwellers. The 'Honey, I'm home' opener adds domestic irony. Good structural payoff on the episode's opening theme.

dialogue.speaker: Uncle Jack
dialogue.line: You know, you and me palling around, getting nuts, doing crazy, fun things... It's stuff that relatives do.

jokes.text: Well, hang on a second, bro. We're good in tight spaces. I'll make it work. / I'm sorry, Charlie. / What do you mean you're sorry? / There's no room at the inn.
jokes.setup: Charlie wants to live in the RV with Frank and Dee.
jokes.punchline: Frank turns Charlie away with 'There's no room at the inn' — a Biblical allusion delivered completely without self-awareness by a man who is now himself a homeless person.
jokes.explanation: Frank using a Biblical innkeeper line while running a shantytown RV is a nice ironic touch. 'There's no room at the inn' from Frank Reynolds is a funny specific choice. Moderate laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Uncle Jack
dialogue.line: You ever seen wrestling on television?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I am well aware of what wrestling is. It's just not what uncles do to their nephews.

jokes.text: Uh, we're not in the business of giving out handouts, Charlie. We're not the government. / Frankly, I'm a little embarrassed that you would ask.
jokes.setup: Charlie, now homeless due to Frank subletting his apartment, asks to live with Dennis and Mac.
jokes.punchline: Dennis invokes anti-government-handout rhetoric to refuse his homeless friend shelter; Mac adds that he's 'embarrassed' Charlie would even ask.
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny cruelty delivered with political framing. Dennis's 'we're not the government' is a sharp piece of character writing — using libertarian talking points to justify abandoning a friend. Mac's affected embarrassment is a good second beat.

dialogue.speaker: Beth
dialogue.line: Actually, I'm vegan.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Okay. Then pretend this shoe is whatever you people eat. Maybe it is a shoe.

jokes.text: It's a little... a little gauche.
jokes.setup: Dennis says he's embarrassed Charlie would ask for shelter.
jokes.punchline: Mac reaches for 'gauche' — a French word indicating social impropriety — to describe a homeless man asking his friends for help.
jokes.explanation: Mac using 'gauche' to describe a homeless man's request is funny in its pretension mismatch. The hesitation before finding the word adds texture.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Owww! Ohh! Is this part of the whole thing? Oh, I cut myself! Ohh! It's a deep cut! I see your bones!

jokes.text: Give me your shoe. / A shoe? / Hand over your shoe. / All right. / Observe... / Wait, no, no, no... / Ah, come on, man! That's a $200 shoe!
jokes.setup: Frank announces his new business plan that will make them rich.
jokes.punchline: Frank's grand business reveal begins with him demanding Dee's shoe and immediately destroying it.
jokes.explanation: Classic Frank energy — the buildup ('feast your eyes') followed by shoe destruction is physically well-executed. Dee's $200 shoe protest adds stakes. The sequence works as physical comedy with good structure.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Oh, shoot! Oh! Oh, I'm missing it! Hey! Oh, no!

dialogue.speaker: Beth
dialogue.line: You're doing that on purpose!

jokes.text: You want me to sell knives door-to-door? / No, you're selling vacuums.
jokes.setup: Frank reveals the business is knives, using Dee's destroyed shoe as a demo.
jokes.punchline: Dee assumes (reasonably) she's selling knives; Frank reveals she's also selling vacuums — the knife demo was apparently just the first half of a two-product door-to-door sales scheme.
jokes.explanation: Good reversal — just as Dee accepts the knife premise, the vacuum is added. The escalating absurdity of Frank's scheme (shoe demo → knife → vacuum) is well-structured escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: See, by transferring all of our cash into these Paddy's Dollars and then printing more of these babies than we ever had in cash, we've upped our value.

jokes.text: Now, cover your ears, because it has no muffler. [industrial vacuum immediately destroys the shoe and carpet while Dee screams]
jokes.setup: Frank is demoing the wet vac's power; has just warned about the noise.
jokes.punchline: The vacuum is catastrophically powerful — it destroys a shoe and apparently a carpet, sending Dee into a panic.
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy that works visually — 'cover your ears' as a warning before chaos is a solid setup. The destruction is clearly over-the-top and plays well on screen even if the transcript minimizes it.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Good-bye, recession, hello, depression. You're very lucky that you're with somebody as resilient as Frank Reynolds.

jokes.text: It's not built for shoes. But look at that rug.
jokes.setup: Frank's industrial vacuum has just caused mayhem in the customer's home.
jokes.punchline: Frank's response to the destruction is a minor product caveat ('not for shoes') followed by a sincere positive redirect to the rug-cleaning results.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Frank Reynolds energy. The cheerful pivot from collateral damage to salesmanship — 'it's not built for shoes. But look at that rug.' — is a gem of deadpan understatement. The 'but look at that rug' is so Frank: genuinely undeterred, finding the silver lining in catastrophe. Very quotable. Earns high craft marks for economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You've tried to off yourself two times in the last 24 hours, Frank!

jokes.text: Oh, that's good Merlot. That's good Merlot. You're gonna want to keep those coming.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are at Dave & Buster's supposedly for a business meeting about saving the bar.
jokes.punchline: Mac is connoisseur-commenting on the wine at Dave & Buster's as if it's a fine restaurant.
jokes.explanation: Mac treating D&B's wine like a sommelier is a consistent thread of the character's delusional self-regard. 'You're gonna want to keep those coming' as a direction to the waitress at an arcade bar is nicely absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: These are crabs! Fresh, local Delaware runoff crabs...

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Yeah, well- They look like sea scorpions.

jokes.text: It might be a little cheaper if you's went with a bottle of wine instead of chugging the individual glasses. / Maybe leave the judgment back in the kitchen.
jokes.setup: Mac is ordering wine by the glass repeatedly at Dave & Buster's.
jokes.punchline: The waitress offers a practical cost-saving tip; Mac tells her to 'leave the judgment back in the kitchen.'
jokes.explanation: 'Leave the judgment back in the kitchen' is a good line — Mac's affected dignity at an arcade restaurant is funny, and telling a waitress to withhold judgment while he chugs D&B wine is suitably absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah, there's a pretty bad sewage runoff, but, you know, crabs is sewage-proof!

jokes.text: Break down for me what I'm holding in my hand right now. / Ah, that is a Dave & Buster's power card.
jokes.setup: Dennis asks Mac to break down what he's holding as if revealing something profound.
jokes.punchline: It's a Dave & Buster's power card — something both men clearly have and use regularly, treated with the gravity of a secret weapon.
jokes.explanation: The solemnity with which Dennis presents an arcade card as a business solution is funny. Sets up the D&B extended riff effectively.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: We're crab people now. We'll live and die by the crab, Dee! We'll eat off the fat of the sea.

jokes.text: Now, does your Dave & Buster's card work at any other similar establishments, like say, TGI Friday's? / Mine does not. Believe me, I've tried at several locations.
jokes.setup: Dennis asks hypothetically whether the D&B power card works elsewhere.
jokes.punchline: Mac answers from personal experience — he has tried the card at multiple TGI Friday's locations and it doesn't work.
jokes.explanation: Mac's immediate, specific personal testimony that he has tried the D&B card 'at several locations' of TGI Friday's is a great character beat. It suggests a whole sad backstory of Mac attempting to use an arcade card at chain restaurants. Very character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: How does this work, Mac? The money keeps moving in a circle. But- But we don't have any money. All we have is this.

jokes.text: Well, yeah. 'Cause if you recall, I've actually been with you on many of those occasions where you've tried.
jokes.setup: Mac reveals he's tried the D&B card at multiple Friday's.
jokes.punchline: Dennis casually reveals he was there with Mac for those attempts — meaning both of them have been repeatedly trying to use an arcade card at TGI Friday's.
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation on the previous joke. Dennis being present at multiple failed D&B card attempts at Friday's implies a whole pathetic history. 'Many of those occasions' implies a truly unreasonable number of tries. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, I blacked out that night. Shit, dude! I've been following your lead!

jokes.text: There's one out in Franklin Mills I haven't tried. / It's not gonna work there either, okay?
jokes.setup: Dennis tells Mac to drop the D&B card/Friday's issue.
jokes.punchline: Mac identifies a specific Friday's location he hasn't yet tried; Dennis shuts it down with certainty.
jokes.explanation: The running gag escalates beautifully — now Mac has a specific location mapped out for his next attempt. Dennis's weary certainty ('it's not gonna work there either') suggests this conversation has happened many times. Great running gag structure.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I don't understand how the U.S. economy works, much less some sort of a self-sustaining one.

jokes.text: And try the card at the 'Friday's out' in the northeast... / No, you son of a bitch. We're way past that at this point.
jokes.setup: Dennis has just pitched the Paddy's Dollars idea and is wrapping up.
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately pivots to suggesting they also try the D&B card at another Friday's location; Dennis erupts.
jokes.explanation: 'No, you son of a bitch. We're way past that at this point.' is Dennis at peak exasperation. Mac's inability to let the Friday's thing go — even mid-business pitch — is a great comedic beat that also characterizes Mac's obsessiveness.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: The government is reimbursing me all the money I lost! I love this country! Baby, I'm back!

jokes.text: And we call it Paddy's dollars. Now, we distribute that out to people for free initially, and then they become customers and then they bring in new customers. And then once they're in, they have to use real dollars to buy Paddy's dollars.
jokes.setup: Dennis presents the bar's economic stimulus plan inspired by Dave & Buster's.
jokes.punchline: The 'Paddy's Dollars' scheme is a transparently obvious pyramid scheme / fake currency — presented by Dennis with complete confidence as economic innovation.
jokes.explanation: The Paddy's Dollars concept is funny as a parody of economic stimulus and corporate loyalty schemes — it's also clearly a fraudulent currency. Dennis's earnest delivery makes it land. The audience understands the scheme is doomed before the characters do.

jokes.text: Yeah, dude, that's a great plan! And then afterwards, we'll go out to fox chase and use the power card at that friday's out there. / Yeah, yeah, yeah. No, we won't. You can, though.
jokes.setup: Mac enthusiastically endorses the Paddy's Dollars plan.
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately follows his endorsement with another Friday's location attempt; Dennis grants permission for Mac to go alone.
jokes.explanation: Dennis's 'No, we won't. You can, though.' is a good subtle joke — he won't go, but he's not going to stop Mac. The running gag is well-worn by now but still delivering because of Dennis's resignation.

jokes.text: Yeah, dude, that's a great plan! And then afterwards, we'll go out to fox chase and use the power card at that Friday's out there. / Yeah, yeah, yeah. No, we won't. You can, though.
jokes.setup: Mac enthusiastically endorses Dennis's Paddy's dollars scheme.
jokes.punchline: Mac appends his endorsement with another Friday's attempt — Fox Chase this time. Dennis's weary 'you can, though' is perfect resignation.
jokes.explanation: Dennis's 'you can, though' is an inspired piece of resigned permissiveness — he has stopped fighting it and is just letting Mac live his truth. The economy of the line is excellent. Good final beat on this running gag before it pays off at the end.

jokes.text: I was figuring maybe I should move back into my old room for a little while till I get back up on my feet. / Well, I don't think that's gonna work out, Charlie. / Why not? / I had to sublet your room to Uncle Jack.
jokes.setup: Charlie, now homeless, asks his mom if he can move back home.
jokes.punchline: His mom has sublet his childhood bedroom — to Uncle Jack, who Charlie clearly has traumatic associations with.
jokes.explanation: The reveal of Uncle Jack as the subletter is a nicely dark joke — the implication being that Charlie's childhood nightmare is now living in his room. Charlie's visible horror and Mom's complete obliviousness plays to the show's dark child-trauma comedy.

jokes.text: Well, I don't think that's gonna work out, Charlie. / Why not? / I had to sublet your room to Uncle Jack. / Is that why he's here? / Hey, Charlie.
jokes.setup: Charlie asks to move back into his childhood room.
jokes.punchline: His room has been given to Uncle Jack — an apparently predatory uncle Charlie spent his childhood avoiding.
jokes.explanation: The reveal of Uncle Jack in Charlie's childhood room is a great dark comedy moment. The implied backstory — why Charlie is so distressed about sharing a room with this uncle — is genuinely disturbing and the show uses that darkness expertly. 'Is that why he's here?' followed by Jack's cheerful 'Hey Charlie' is perfectly timed.

jokes.text: What are you talking about? You don't make house payments. You own this house. You've owned it for years. / Mom, that's crazy. You collect social security!
jokes.setup: Charlie's mom explains she sublet his room because she needs money for 'house payments.'
jokes.punchline: Charlie points out she owns the house outright and collects Social Security — the financial reasoning is entirely fabricated.
jokes.explanation: Functional but relatively mild. Charlie's mom's financial confusion is a background joke. The scene's real humor is the Uncle Jack situation.

jokes.text: You can share the room with me, Charlie. / That's a great idea! / That is not a great idea.
jokes.setup: Charlie refuses to move back because Uncle Jack has his room.
jokes.punchline: Uncle Jack enthusiastically invites Charlie to share the room; Mom agrees; Charlie's horror escalates.
jokes.explanation: The three-way split — Uncle Jack's enthusiasm, Mom's obliviousness, Charlie's vehement refusal — is a well-structured comedic three-beat. The dark implication of why Charlie refuses is what gives it depth.

jokes.text: It'll be fine. You and me palling around... getting nuts, doing crazy, fun things.
jokes.setup: Uncle Jack tries to sell Charlie on sharing the room.
jokes.punchline: 'Getting nuts, doing crazy, fun things' — delivered by a character with clearly predatory overtones toward Charlie — is horrifying in context.
jokes.explanation: Uncle Jack's cheerful vagueness about 'crazy, fun things' is played as deeply sinister. The cringe here comes from implication — the audience fills in the blanks. Good dark comedy economy.

jokes.text: I don't want to share a room with you, dude, because I will spend the whole night wide awake, just like when I was a kid and you tried to share my room.
jokes.setup: Uncle Jack pressures Charlie to share the room.
jokes.punchline: Charlie reveals this has happened before — Uncle Jack 'tried to share his room' as a child, keeping Charlie awake all night.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's matter-of-fact recounting of childhood trauma is played for dark laughs. His statement that he 'will spend the whole night wide awake' is played completely seriously, which makes it funnier. Strong character integration with Charlie's traumatic backstory.

jokes.text: You ever seen wrestling on television? / I'm well aware of what wrestling is. It's just not what uncles do to their nephews.
jokes.setup: Uncle Jack tries to explain what the 'crazy fun things' are.
jokes.punchline: Uncle Jack's euphemism for predatory behavior is 'wrestling on television'; Charlie immediately and correctly identifies that wrestling is not standard uncle-nephew activity.
jokes.explanation: One of the funnier Uncle Jack moments. The 'wrestling on television' euphemism is exactly the kind of oblique predatory suggestion the character would make, and Charlie's response — 'I'm well aware of what wrestling is. It's just not what uncles do to their nephews' — is a perfect comeback that acknowledges the subtext while maintaining plausible deniability. The rhythm of the exchange is excellent.

jokes.text: Hey, I'll call you later. / I know you will.
jokes.setup: Charlie is fleeing the house to escape Uncle Jack.
jokes.punchline: Uncle Jack says he'll call later; Charlie's flat 'I know you will' implies resigned acceptance of this inevitability.
jokes.explanation: Four words of perfect economy. Charlie's 'I know you will' — delivered with resigned certainty — is a great button on the Uncle Jack scene. The implication is bleak and funny simultaneously.

jokes.text: Actually, I'm vegan. / Okay, then pretend this shoe is whatever you people eat. / Maybe it is a shoe. / Nice one.
jokes.setup: Frank tells the customer to pretend the shoe is an unboned chicken they're going to cook for dinner.
jokes.punchline: The customer reveals she's vegan; Frank's adaptation is to suggest the shoe IS what vegans eat; the customer fires back 'maybe it is a shoe'; Dee compliments the comeback.
jokes.explanation: Frank's 'whatever you people eat' is a great casual insult, then the customer's comeback — 'Maybe it is a shoe' — landing well enough that Dee breaks to compliment it ('Nice one') is a fun three-part structure. The customer winning an exchange against Frank is an unexpected pleasure.

jokes.text: Oh, it's just flopping around. It's, like, not even making a dent in the leather. This knife is a piece of crap.
jokes.setup: Frank is demonstrating the knife's sharpness to a potential customer.
jokes.punchline: The 'sharpest knife from the bar' is completely useless — it can't cut a shoe, destroying the entire sales pitch in real time.
jokes.explanation: Frank's self-sabotaging sales demo continues to escalate. His candid assessment of his own product ('this knife is a piece of crap') is funny in its honesty, though the joke is a bit predictable.

jokes.text: Frank cuts himself deeply with the demo knife while trying to cut the shoe.
jokes.setup: Frank has switched to the 'good' knife to demonstrate its superior quality.
jokes.punchline: Frank immediately cuts himself — deeply, to the bone — with the knife he's been praising.
jokes.explanation: Classic slapstick escalation — the product you're selling injures the salesman. Predictable but physically executed well. The 'I see your bones' line from Dee elevates it slightly.

jokes.text: I see your bones.
jokes.setup: Frank has cut himself severely with the knife.
jokes.punchline: Dee's reaction to Frank's deep wound is the clinical observation 'I see your bones' — not screaming or concern, just a visual report.
jokes.explanation: Four words that earn their laugh entirely on economy and deadpan delivery. 'I see your bones' is said with zero emotional reaction, which is the whole joke. It's specific, visual, and surprisingly quotable. Dee's detachment from Frank's injury is perfectly on-brand. One of the most memorable lines in the episode.

jokes.text: Why don't you and I have a glass of wine, just bring it down a little bit, huh? / I don't drink in the morning. / Yeah, me neither.
jokes.setup: Dee tries to calm the traumatized customer after Frank bleeds all over her house.
jokes.punchline: Dee suggests morning wine; the customer declines because it's morning; Dee also claims not to drink in the morning — immediately after ordering wine earlier.
jokes.explanation: Dee's immediate 'yeah, me neither' after suggesting morning wine is a quick, clean hypocrisy joke. Good economy.

jokes.text: Oh, shoot. Oh! Oh, I'm missing it! / Oh, no! / You're doing that on purpose. / I'm trying to prove a point here, Beth.
jokes.setup: Dee is demonstrating the wet vac's power to the customer after Frank's injury.
jokes.punchline: Dee is apparently failing spectacularly to control the vacuum — missing whatever she's trying to clean up, with the customer accusing her of doing it deliberately.
jokes.explanation: Inferred physical comedy — Dee's vacuum demo going badly while she insists she's making a point. Moderate laugh, slightly unclear from transcript alone.

jokes.text: These Paddy's dollars look great, bro. Yeah. I'm really glad we went with the color. They pop! / A little bit more expensive than I would've thought. But that's worth it, though. / That's an old poor move.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are examining the printed Paddy's Dollars.
jokes.punchline: They've apparently spent significant money printing fake currency — and frame the expense as a sign of sophistication ('they pop'; 'that's an old poor move').
jokes.explanation: A callback to the 'old poor' distinction — Mac and Dennis invocating it to justify spending money they don't have on printed fake money is a good ironic beat. 'They pop' about counterfeit currency is a fun detail.

jokes.text: See, by transferring all of our cash into these Paddy's dollars and then printing more of these babies than we ever had in cash, we've upped our value.
jokes.setup: Mac explains the Paddy's Dollars economic theory.
jokes.punchline: Mac describes converting all real cash into fake currency and then printing MORE fake money as 'upping their value' — a perfect parody of financial nonsense.
jokes.explanation: Mac accidentally describes hyper-inflation and currency fraud as an economic win. It's a sharp parody of the kind of financial gibberish that caused the actual 2008 recession, delivered by a moron with complete confidence.

jokes.text: In recession times, what thrives more than anything else? / Prostitutes. / No — well, yeah, but that and bars.
jokes.setup: Mac is building to his point about recession economics.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's first answer to 'what thrives in a recession' is 'prostitutes' — and Mac's response is 'no — well, yeah, but that AND bars.'
jokes.explanation: One of the best exchanges in the episode. 'Prostitutes' as the first answer is unexpected but immediately makes sense. Mac's correction — 'no — well, yeah, but that AND bars' — is a perfect concession that validates both answers. The rhythm of the exchange is tight and quotable. Classic Always Sunny darkness delivered with economy.

jokes.text: When people stop buying vacuum cleaners and knives door to door, it could mean only one thing, Deandra. / That you blew all of my money on a very stupid idea? / No. Good-bye recession, hello, depression.
jokes.setup: Frank and Dee's door-to-door venture has completely failed.
jokes.punchline: Dee correctly identifies the obvious conclusion (stupid idea); Frank reframes total market failure as macro-economic evidence of a deepening depression.
jokes.explanation: 'Good-bye recession, hello, depression' is an excellent Frank line. The misdirect works perfectly: Dee identifies the obvious truth; Frank completely ignores it and reframes his failure as economic analysis. The phrase itself is punchy and quotable. Strong structure.

jokes.text: You're very lucky that you're with somebody as resilient as Frank Reynolds. / You tried to off yourself two times in the last 24 hours, Frank.
jokes.setup: Frank delivers a motivational speech about his resilience.
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately deflates it by reminding him he's attempted suicide twice today.
jokes.explanation: A great callback delivered with perfect Dee timing. Frank's self-aggrandizement ('somebody as resilient as Frank Reynolds') punctured by the specificity of 'two times in the last 24 hours' is excellent. The casualness of recounting suicide attempts as a conversational rebuttal is quintessential Always Sunny.

jokes.text: His business partner called. / This is the man who's going to make us rich. / [cut to: man living in a cardboard box] / Times is tough.
jokes.setup: Frank announces his new brilliant business partner with great fanfare.
jokes.punchline: The partner lives in a cardboard box in the shantytown.
jokes.explanation: Classic visual reveal joke — build up the partner, cut to cardboard box. Frank's 'Times is tough' is a good button that also reveals he has zero self-awareness about the situation.

jokes.text: Charlie is Frank's new business partner. / Yeah, well, what do you want? I mean, we're good in tight spots.
jokes.setup: Frank reveals his business partner is Charlie — who was just fired from the bar and is now homeless.
jokes.punchline: Frank's explanation: 'we're good in tight spots' — an expression meaning pressure situations, but also literally true as they both just tried to squeeze into a small RV.
jokes.explanation: A callback on 'good in tight spaces/spots' — the phrase applied now to their current predicament works on both levels. Good economy.

jokes.text: What the hell is that? / These are crabs. Fresh, local Delaware runoff crabs. / Those don't look anything like crabs. They look like sea scorpions.
jokes.setup: Frank and Charlie present their new business plan with great enthusiasm.
jokes.punchline: The business plan is selling crabs from Delaware sewage runoff — crabs that look like sea scorpions.
jokes.explanation: 'Fresh, local Delaware runoff crabs' is a great phrase — the word 'fresh' doing enormous ironic work next to 'runoff.' 'They look like sea scorpions' adds a vivid, gross detail. Good dark food comedy.

jokes.text: Isn't there some kind of, like, sewage runoff around here? / You know, crabs is sewage-proof. And depression-proof. People got to eat.
jokes.setup: Dee notes the obvious health concern with Delaware runoff crabs.
jokes.punchline: Frank asserts crabs are 'sewage-proof' as a matter of fact, then pivots to a macro-economic argument for selling contaminated seafood.
jokes.explanation: 'Crabs is sewage-proof' is a baffling and funny statement delivered with absolute confidence. The escalation to 'depression-proof. People got to eat.' applies real economic logic (necessity goods) to inedible sewage crabs. Very Frank — his logic is impeccable within its own insane frame. Quotable.

jokes.text: We're crab people now. / Crab people. / We're crab people now? / You want us to become crab people?
jokes.setup: Frank announces they'll sell crabs on the street.
jokes.punchline: Charlie declares 'We're crab people now' with sincere gravity; Frank echoes it; Dee's horror at the new identity is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable moments in the episode. 'Crab people' as an identity category — declared solemnly by Charlie — is a perfect absurdist character beat. The repetition and Dee's existential horror ('You want us to become crab people?') gives it escalating weight. The phrase itself is ridiculous and memorable.

jokes.text: We'll live and die by the crab, Dee. We'll eat off the fat of the sea.
jokes.setup: Dee is horrified at becoming 'crab people.'
jokes.punchline: Frank delivers a solemn, almost poetic declaration of their new crab-based existence — 'We'll live and die by the crab' — with the gravity of a mob oath.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. 'We'll live and die by the crab, Dee' is delivered with the seriousness of a warrior's creed — applied to selling sewage crabs on the street. 'Eat off the fat of the sea' is a beautiful Steinbeck/Of Mice and Men parody. The language elevates the absurdity beautifully. Highly quotable, strong character integration with Frank's delusional grandeur.

jokes.text: Hey, will you help me toss some of these babies back, 'cause legally we're not allowed to eat those.
jokes.setup: Frank and Charlie are proudly displaying their crab business.
jokes.punchline: Charlie casually reveals the crabs are legally prohibited for human consumption — information he delivers while trying to get rid of them.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's matter-of-fact acknowledgment that the crabs are legally inedible — immediately after establishing a whole business plan around them — is a great beat. The reveal is casual, which makes it land harder.

jokes.text: Hey, I think we made every single one of our Paddy's dollars back, buddy. / You're damn right. Thus creating the self-sustaining economy we've been looking for.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis have distributed Paddy's Dollars to the shantytown and people spent them on drinks.
jokes.punchline: Their triumph is that they made back all their fake money — no actual US dollars exchanged — which they frame as a successful economy.
jokes.explanation: The 'self-sustaining economy' callback works because they've technically achieved it — but only within their own worthless currency. The delusion is complete and consistent.

jokes.text: Fresh cash? / Uh, well, zero — zero if you're talking about US currency.
jokes.setup: Dennis asks how much 'fresh cash' they made from the Paddy's Dollars distribution.
jokes.punchline: Mac's answer is zero — clarified specifically as 'zero if you're talking about US currency' — implying there might be a currency in which they broke even.
jokes.explanation: The qualifier 'if you're talking about US currency' is the whole joke — it implies Mac has been mentally working in Paddy's Dollars, a currency he created and controls. The hedge is both delusional and logically consistent with how he's been thinking.

jokes.text: I blacked out. I blacked out that night. / Shit, dude, I've been following your lead. / Oh, Jesus. Oh, shit.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis try to work out how their Paddy's Dollars economy actually functions.
jokes.punchline: Dennis reveals he was blacked out when he came up with the plan — meaning the entire Paddy's Dollars scheme was designed by a drunk person and Mac followed it unquestioningly.
jokes.explanation: A great structural revelation. The entire Paddy's Dollars scheme was blackout-planned and followed by Mac who thought Dennis knew what he was doing. 'I've been following your lead' + 'I blacked out' is a perfect double revelation. The 'Oh, Jesus. Oh, shit.' from Dennis acknowledging the full scale of the problem is funny in its belated panic.

jokes.text: How does D&B's do it? They've got a complicated system worked out, and I cannot begin to understand it. / How does a self-sustaining economy work? / I don't understand how the US economy works, much less some sort of self-sustaining one. / I don't understand how finances work.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis realize their Paddy's Dollars scheme has completely collapsed.
jokes.punchline: Their post-mortem reveals a cascade of ignorance — neither understands Dave & Buster's economics, the US economy, or finance in general.
jokes.explanation: The cascading admissions of total financial ignorance ('I don't understand the US economy... I don't understand how finances work') is a great escalating confession. It characterizes both men perfectly and also functions as sharp satire of people who caused the actual recession.

jokes.text: I don't understand how the US economy works, much less some sort of self-sustaining one.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are trying to understand why their fake economy failed.
jokes.punchline: Mac's honest admission that he doesn't understand either the real economy or their fake one — delivered as a simple confession after they've executed an elaborate financial scheme.
jokes.explanation: Good honest deflation. The simplicity of Mac just admitting total ignorance after a whole episode of elaborate scheming is well-timed. 'Much less some sort of self-sustaining one' is a nicely humble addendum.

jokes.text: Shots for everybody! The government is reimbursing me all the money I lost. I love this country.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are in existential financial crisis.
jokes.punchline: Frank explodes in with news that the government bailed him out — perfectly satirizing actual 2008 bank bailouts.
jokes.explanation: Frank's triumphant reentry with government bailout news is a sharp piece of political satire — the morally bankrupt, literally suicidal rich man gets bailed out by the government while the working-class bar suffers. 'I love this country!' is the perfect exclamation point. Timely, earned, and character-specific.

jokes.text: Can you bail us out, Frank? 'Cause we're kind of screwed here. / I'll tell you what, let's discuss it over steaks and skee balls.
jokes.setup: Mac asks Frank for a bailout after their Paddy's Dollars disaster.
jokes.punchline: Frank responds with Dave & Buster's — full circle from the opening D&B scene.
jokes.explanation: The D&B callback in the bailout context works because Frank — who earlier complained about steak expenses — is now the one suggesting it. The irony of the bailout enabling the same behavior Frank criticized is a good structural payoff.

jokes.text: USA! USA! USA! USA! / I love this country. / Crab meat... Crab meat...
jokes.setup: Frank announces the bailout and suggests Dave & Buster's.
jokes.punchline: The whole gang erupts into 'USA! USA!' chants — including Charlie murmuring 'crab meat' — as a parody of American exceptionalism during a financial crisis.
jokes.explanation: The 'USA!' chants are a sharp satirical button on the bailout, and Charlie's 'crab meat... crab meat...' murmured underneath is a perfect character-specific detail — he's already mentally back on the crab business even during the celebration. Good ensemble moment.

jokes.text: Uh, you guys don't think that you're going to Dave & Buster's, do you?
jokes.setup: Frank has just invited everyone to celebrate with steaks and skee balls at D&B's.
jokes.punchline: Mac — one of D&B's most devoted patrons, who has been trying to use a D&B card at Friday's the whole episode — acts like Dave & Buster's is beneath consideration at the last moment.
jokes.explanation: The final D&B callback is a great episode button. Mac — who has spent the entire episode obsessing over D&B — now acts as if it's not up to their standards. It's a funny character contradiction that closes the D&B running gag. The deadpan 'you guys don't think' implies he now considers himself above it.

tmdb_overview: With a shantytown taking shape outside, Mac and Dennis try to keep Paddy's going in tough times. Meanwhile, Frank and Dee start a family business.
